The Fed Just Warned That AI Could Trigger a Bank Run Faster Than Any Human Could Possibly Stop It

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The arrival of AI can be summed up in one word: instability.
  • Recent findings suggest that now there’s another worry to add to the list: bank runs.
  • “AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods,” Barr mentioned in his speech.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The arrival of AI can be summed up in one word: instability. Since ChatGPT brought large language models (LLMs) into the mainstream in late 2022, instability in the job market has been a given. As the technology has required more and more resources, instability in utilities’ ability to supply power also became painfully clear. And as AI companies’ valuations skyrocketed in recent years, worries of an AI bubble have highlighted the instability of millions of retirement plans.

Recent findings suggest that now there’s another worry to add to the list: bank runs. In a speech in Milan last week, Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr warned that AI’s ability to react to a financial crisis at unprecedented speed could make future runs far more devastating.

“AI agents may accelerate deposit outflows during stress periods,” Barr mentioned in his speech. “Where customers once needed to execute transfers, AI agents could instantaneously detect yield differentials or stability signals and autonomously move funds at high speed, potentially accelerating runs that unfold in minutes, overwhelming traditional liquidity management and regulatory intervention timelines.”.

Bank runs have been a fixture of U.S. financial crises since the Panic of 1792, when the newly independent country’s government was a whopping three years old. Banks don’t keep enough cash on hand to cover every deposit, but instead use that cash for loans and investments. But if the job or stock market takes a turn for the worse, customers might attempt to withdraw funds all at once, forcing banks to sell off investments at a loss, pushing them toward insolvency. After widespread bank failures during the Great Depression, the U.S. government created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) to protect depositors. The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, serves as lender of last resort, providing emergency loans to banks experiencing runs.

Sources indicate that these failsafes have typically operated at the speed of a human. But in a world where AI can pour gasoline on a financial panic by accelerating withdrawals upon detecting telltale instability in markets, bank runs could unfold in mere minutes.

And that isn’t the only concern AI presents to the banking world. Bank executives told Axios in late October that banks are struggling to distinguish between AI bots and human owners, prompting them to restrict third-party AI access to their platforms. Major banks such as JPMorgan Chase, Citi, and Bank of America have already done so.

Sources indicate that “We strongly believe there should be a human in the loop to authorize money moving out of your account,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC last month. “We’re working with the agentic agent providers to say, ‘Hey, you really don’t want consumers coming back and say money moved over from my account and I don’t know why and I don’t know where it went and the agent did it.’”.

The swift efficiency of AI agents, tasked with squeezing every possible cent from a customer’s money, means they could also move money from non-interest-bearing deposits (such as a checking account) into high-yield accounts paying upwards of 5 percent. The problem is that banks rely on low-interest accounts to fund loans, so a sudden exodus would inject unwanted volatility into the financial system.

The second most common element in the universe is actually running out here on Earth

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space.
  • According to recent reports, most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space.
  • The British scientist Norman Lockyer named the mystery substance helium after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun, as recounted by the American Physical Society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious….

According to recent reports, most of the elements we rely on were found underground, but helium was first discovered in space. In 1868, astronomers studying a total solar eclipse spotted a mysterious yellow band in the Sun’s light spectrum that did not match any known element.

The British scientist Norman Lockyer named the mystery substance helium after Helios, the Greek god of the Sun, as recounted by the American Physical Society.

Humanity had identified an element in starlight 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) away before anyone held a sample of it.

Recent findings suggest that confirmation took decades. The Scottish chemist William Ramsay finally isolated terrestrial helium in 1895, releasing it from a uranium-bearing mineral nearly 27 years after Lockyer first saw its signature.

In a recent development, that long delay hints at the problem now reshaping hospitals and laboratories. Helium is the second-most-abundant element in the universe, yet it is genuinely rare on Earth.

The contradiction comes down to gravity. Helium is so light that it drifts upward, escapes the atmosphere, and is lost to space forever. Our Moon even collects traces of the gases our planet sheds. The cosmic abundance simply never settled here.

According to recent reports, the helium we use does not come from the Big Bang reservoir that fills the cosmos. It forms underground, atom by atom, as radioactive uranium and thorium decay within the crust.

According to recent reports, those elements decay on almost unimaginable timescales. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years and thorium-232 closer to 14 billion years, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. Each decay releases the alpha particles that become helium.

The same slow chemistry that shaped Earth’s crust over billions of years also governs its helium. No factory can shortcut that process, which is why no large-scale method exists to manufacture the gas artificially.

In a recent development, this is the deeper reason the current squeeze matters. A shortfall in most materials invites more mining or more production. A helium shortfall invites neither, because the planet replenishes its supply only as fast as atoms decay.

Producers extract helium as a trace component of natural gas, and only deposits with high enough concentrations are worth tapping. That narrow geology leaves the market exposed to plant shutdowns and trade disruptions.

The strain is already visible. Hospitals consume roughly a third of the world’s helium to cool the superconducting magnets in MRI scanners, and analysts expect global demand to double by 2035 as semiconductor and electric-vehicle manufacturing expand.

The hunt for fresh supply is reaching parts of the world that never produced helium before. In Tanzania, the Southern Rukwa project finalized its mining agreements in May 2026, positioning the country to extract helium at a commercial scale. Qatar has also moved to bring fresh capacity online.

Industry observers note that policy decisions have added uncertainty. The United States sold its Federal Helium System, once the planet’s largest single source, to the industrial gas company Messer in June 2024, ending nearly a century of public stewardship, the U.S. Bureau of Land Management confirmed.

Industry observers note that newer MRI machines now seal and recirculate their helium, and many labs capture and re-liquefy every drop they can. These measures buy time, much as a simple scan can buy a patient time. Whether they arrive fast enough is the open question.

Sources indicate that there is a quiet symmetry to the helium story. We discovered it by looking up at a star, much as a meteorite can reveal a vanished world, and we may yet preserve it by looking down into the rocks that hoard it.

In a recent development, for now, the element that fills birthday balloons remains one of the most strategically notable substances on the planet. It reminds us that some of Earth’s rarest things are those we first noticed in the heavens.

The full study was published in the journal Physics Today.

Crews tearing up a 1950s parking lot at Dinosaur National Monument hit fossils, but the real find was a dinosaur tail with nine vertebrae

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.
  • In September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park.
  • Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Under a Dinosaur National Monument parking lot, a paleontologist found a likely Diplodocus tail with nine vertebrae in the first dig there since 1924.

In September 2025, road crews at Dinosaur National Monument in Utah peeled back the asphalt outside the Quarry Exhibit Hall, the most popular stop in the park. They were there to rebuild a parking lot. The first scoop of the backhoe brought up pieces of fossil bone.

Over the next five weeks, the job turned into a dinosaur dig.

Park paleontologist ReBecca Hunt-Foster and her assistant followed a trail of bones through the rock until they had uncovered nine tail vertebrae and the leg and arm bones of a long-necked dinosaur, most likely Diplodocus.

Its relatives still turn up in surprising places, including the first Diplodocus ever found outside North America.

It has been revealed that it was the first fossil excavation in that part of the historic Carnegie Quarry since 1924, the National Park Service stated. In an account published this fall, Hunt-Foster described how the last bones of the tail were lying right against the old asphalt.

In a recent development, the spot has a long history. On August 17, 1909, Earl Douglass, a paleontologist from the Carnegie Museum in Pittsburgh, spotted eight dinosaur tailbones sticking out of a sandstone ledge in the Utah desert. “It was a beautiful sight,” he wrote in his diary.

His crews spent the next 13 years digging there and collected more than 317 metric tons of fossils and rock between 1909 and 1922, according to Hunt-Foster, much of it shipped back to Pittsburgh.

Recent findings suggest that the Smithsonian dug on the east side of the quarry in 1923, and the University of Utah in 1924. In 1915, President Woodrow Wilson set aside the quarry and 80 acres around it as Dinosaur National Monument.

All that digging produced a lot of waste rock. It was dumped off the eastern side of the quarry, and in the 1930s, New Deal work crews cleared more debris while improving the road.

Those tailing piles later became the parking lot for the Quarry Exhibit Hall, which opened in 1958 around a wall of rock where visitors can see about 1,500 dinosaur fossils still in place.

In May 2025, the park was due to begin an $11.2 million project to upgrade roads, parking areas and overlooks along the route to the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

Because the work crossed fossil-bearing rock, the park brought on a seasonal paleontological assistant, Rudolph Hummel, to watch the construction.

It has been revealed that the biggest worry was the parking lot. Fossils overlooked by the early excavators, or judged not worth keeping, could be sitting in the old tailings. The bone-bearing sandstone itself might also turn up.

Recent findings suggest that the road and the exhibit hall closed from September 8 to late October 2025. Monitoring in the parking lot began on September 10, after the asphalt cap came off.

On September 11, the team found the first identifiable bone, a vertebra from a meat-eating dinosaur, likely Allosaurus. Smaller finds followed every day as the crew dug down five feet. Construction sites have a way of turning up fossils, as a Los Angeles project showed.

In a recent development, the construction workers got caught up in it too. Many of them jumped in to search for fossils by hand rather than by backhoe alone, Hunt-Foster wrote, and one worker spent two days power-washing a section of the sandstone so it could be studied.

On September 16, after that washing was done, Hunt-Foster was documenting the exposed sandstone when she spotted a fossil bone in its cross section.

Sources indicate that it turned out to be a large limb bone plunging down into the rock. Construction in that corner of the lot was paused.

After a week of digging, the pair found a tail vertebra lying over the long bone, which they identified as a sauropod tibia. Then a second vertebra appeared, and a third, all still connected. Hummel followed them east while Hunt-Foster worked west.

Six more tail vertebrae turned up, along with the bones of the lower arm. By then, the team had concluded that the tail likely belonged to Diplodocus, the most abundant dinosaur in the Carnegie Quarry.

They also found a partial turtle, plenty of freshwater clams and carbonized wood lying directly under the skeleton.

By September 26, the team had reached the end of the tail. The vertebrae grew smaller toward the east, and the last one was missing its back half, cleanly sheared off and tilted up toward the old surface.

According to recent reports, hunt-Foster and Hummel suspect that the tip of the tail, if it was preserved at all, was plowed off when the road was first built in the late 1950s. Several of the last vertebrae were in direct contact with the asphalt from the lot’s first paving.

Photos from the visitor center’s opening on June 1, 1958, show the lot was still gravel, and it does not appear to have been paved until around 1959, she wrote.

All of this happened while the upcoming parking lot was being built around the dig. Dump trucks full of fill rolled past and rollers packed down the ground around them. “In a short amount of time, we were sitting in a deep trench surrounded by a fresh parking lot,” Hunt-Foster wrote.

Volunteers, a Utah Conservation Corps crew, park coworkers and construction staff helped wrap the bones in protective field jackets. The first small jacket came out on October 13. On October 17, the construction crew’s backhoe operator lifted out the rest.

In all, about 3,000 pounds of fossils and rock came out of the 2025 dig. The bones are now being cleaned and studied at the Utah Field House of Natural History State Park Museum in Vernal, Utah.

Visitors can watch the work in the museum’s fossil preparation lab. Some fossils from the excavation are also on display at the Quarry Exhibit Hall.

The parking lot is finished, and the Quarry Exhibit Hall is open daily except on Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day.

Sources indicate that the story is not over. Hunt-Foster says a second part of her account will cover continued excavation work in 2026 and additional discoveries.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s January 2026 announcement of the excavation, ReBecca Hunt-Foster’s article The Parking Lot Sauropod of Dinosaur National Monument: Part 1 in Park Paleontology News, and the park’s pages on Earl Douglass and the historic Carnegie Quarry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • There’s a quote often falsely attributed to Vladimir Lenin that “There are decades where nothing happens; and there are weeks where decades happen.” The cybersecurity world experienced one of those weeks earlier this month, and the ramifications have sent shockwaves through the halls of government and the average American home.
  • Was this an anomaly, or the first sign of an anarchic AI-fueled collapse?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There’s a quote often falsely attributed to Vladimir Lenin that “There are decades where nothing happens; and there are weeks where decades happen.” The cybersecurity world experienced one of those weeks earlier this month, and the ramifications have sent shockwaves through the halls of government and the average American home.

Was this an anomaly, or the first sign of an anarchic AI-fueled collapse?

People were already grumbling that the AI bubble was about to burst when the story of then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged indiscretions broke. Then, on November 12, Microsoft suffered a massive outage, hobbling an email service countless companies rely on. The next day, just as people’s inboxes were finally refilling, the FAA began grounding airplanes nationwide due to some unspecified computer error.

The demon in the machine evidently took the weekend off but came back with a vengeance on Monday. That’s when major disruptions hit banks like Chase, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America. America had been hit in its workplace, its skies, and even its pocketbook, but the final blow (for now) struck at a spot most Americans will never even see. On November 17, reports emerged that a significant outage had struck the NSA’s own internal, heavily classified network.

After that, the conversation shifted. People were no longer wondering whether the AI bubble would burst; they were asking whether AI would take us down with it.

Sources indicate that in the aftermath, Congress decided there was no choice but to act. It was time to finally take a stand on AI that would prevent these kinds of outages in the future, even if nobody was terribly clear on just what had caused these disruptions, or what exactly AI had to do with them. There were bipartisan calls to assemble the “Superintelligence Task Force” to combat cyberattacks, and a series of amendments was proposed for the National Defense Authorization Act to limit China’s access to American chip-making tools, curbing its ability to produce malicious AI.

In a recent development, but what if we’re thinking about this all wrong? What if AI wasn’t attacking us at all? Maybe the AI was just doing its job, trying to strengthen our defenses, and its well-intentioned efforts had devastating consequences.

According to recent reports, “Nobody ever asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?” Nicole Perlroth, a cybersecurity journalist and author of the book This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: The Cyberweapons Arms Race, wrote in a thread on X. “We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability.”.

Perlroth argued that the official story being put forward by the affected institutions, that the outages were due to patch issues rather than overt cyberattacks, isn’t a lie, and that’s precisely the problem.

What Perlroth posited in her thread, later supported by reporting in The Washington Sun, was that the AI these organizations had integrated into their systems had become efficient at finding critical vulnerabilities. Too efficient, actually. AI, it seems, had found “3X the number of vulnerabilities discovered in the same period last year.” On the surface, that might seem like a good thing. But it’s not enough to simply identify a weak spot—you also have to fix it before anybody else finds it.

According to recent reports, “Mean time to exploit those vulnerabilities has collapsed to NEGATIVE SEVEN DAYS,” Perlroth wrote. “AI allows attackers to find/exploit vulns far faster than software makers have time to fix them.” Offensive AI tools like ARTEX can play a role in that exploitation, Perlroth acknowledged, but what’s likely playing a bigger role in these system outages isn’t an outside invader, but rather the system unintentionally damaging itself in a misguided attempt to patch the weak spots.

The rapid AI-powered discovery of these vulnerabilities “creates enormous pressure to compress patching windows and accelerate software updates,” Perlroth noted, “increasing the likelihood these fixes break things in unexpected, cascading ways.” In effect, the Silicon Valley adage of “move fast and break things” steamrolled the the principle of “first, do no harm,” long associated with the Hippocratic Oath.

It has been revealed that perhaps that ancient oath of physicians should make a comeback as we move into this upcoming age of technology. After all, we’ve used medical terms for technological matters before; even the most “seasoned” senators and congresspeople on Capitol Hill have heard of a computer “virus.” That’s likely the framework lawmakers are using as they try to legislate the genie back into the bottle.

Recent findings suggest that but a virus is a foreign agent, an outside entity that creeps into the body and wreaks havoc. What appears to be happening with the AI-associated outages we just experienced is more akin to a different medical concern: an autoimmune disease. In those instances, it is the body’s own immune system that, in a misguided effort to protect itself, mistakes healthy cells for harmful foreign agents and winds up damaging the body it’s intended to defend.

In the rush to repair these AI-identified vulnerabilities, The Washington Sun summarized, the organizations are “trying to push through a lot of patches all at once—more than the system was designed for,” and in doing so, are introducing entirely new flaws and bugs.

Knowing exactly what you’re dealing with can make all the difference when you’re trying to fix a problem, whether it’s in the human body or in a computer system. A misdiagnosis on either front can have catastrophic consequences.

Let’s hope our lawmakers and engineers have brushed up on their digital pathology.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that it was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

It has been revealed that in September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

Recent findings suggest that 2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the Newly introduced Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

Industry observers note that the heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

Industry News: Possible new dwarf planet that is roughly 930 miles wide had gone unnoticed in telescope images since 2016

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Vera C.
  • A distant object named 2026 ED138 may be a dwarf planet between 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 kilometers) wide, the Vera C.
  • Archival images show that another instrument, the Dark Energy Camera, had recorded it since February 25, 2016, without anyone noticing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory discovered 2026 ED138, a distant dwarf planet candidate beyond Neptune whose size and shape remain unconfirmed.

A distant object named 2026 ED138 may be a dwarf planet between 370 and 930 miles (600 and 1,500 kilometers) wide, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory unveiled on October 27, 2026.

Archival images show that another instrument, the Dark Energy Camera, had recorded it since February 25, 2016, without anyone noticing.

The object remains a candidate because its size has been estimated, not measured.

Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, found the object on the evening of October 13. He was running Rubin data collected earlier in 2026 through a search code developed with colleague Kevin Napier.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman stated.

“Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong,” he added.

The code first detected a cluster of ten observations on eight nights. Mario Jurić, Rubin’s solar system lead scientist at the University of Washington, then found 20 more in Rubin’s catalogs and images.

Industry observers note that in all, the observatory’s telescope saw the object 30 times on 20 nights between March 4 and July 11. The results were presented at a planetary science meeting in Spokane, Washington.

“It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years,” Jurić said.

The object is right now about 46 astronomical units from the Sun, or roughly 4.3 billion miles (6.9 billion kilometers). Pluto averages 39 of those units, each equal to Earth’s distance from the Sun, by NASA‘s figures.

According to recent reports, its orbit, which comes no closer to the Sun than about 37 astronomical units, is tilted almost 25 degrees from the solar system’s plane. The announcement suggests that gravitational interactions with Neptune disturbed the object’s original path.

Sources indicate that earlier surveys missed 2026 ED138 because it lies far south and near the crowded regions of the Galactic plane, the discovery paper states. In April, Rubin had already submitted observations of more than 11,000 new asteroids.

Given the orbit computed from Rubin data alone, an archive search service returned older candidate detections. The object appears in 45 Dark Energy Camera exposures on 14 nights, the last on April 7, 2023.

“Once we identify a upcoming object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look,” Jurić explained.

It has been revealed that A century-long archival search, posted on November 2 and not yet peer-reviewed, pushes the record back further. It reports the object on 12 photographic plates taken between 1954 and 2000, plus a marginal detection on a 1937 plate.

It has been revealed that the diameter is calculated from the object’s brightness and an assumed albedo, the fraction of sunlight its surface reflects. That albedo has not been measured.

Sources indicate that the upper end of the announced range requires a very dark surface, one that reflects only four percent of the light. A diameter between 380 and 600 miles (612 and 968 kilometers) is more probable, by the discoverers’ own assessment.

Pluto, Eris and Makemake, whose surfaces are rich in methane ice, reflect about 60 to 90 percent of sunlight. So bright a surface is considered less likely for 2026 ED138, although its composition is still unknown.

It has been revealed that “Thermal photometry or a stellar occultation is needed to decide between these sizes,” the authors wrote. An occultation occurs when an object passes in front of a star and briefly blocks its light.

The archival study predicts 15 such events between 2027 and 2030, six of them over populated land. It also reports a tentative rotation signal with a period of 10.4 hours.

By intrinsic brightness, the object ranks ninth or tenth among known bodies beyond Neptune, depending on which measurements are compared.

Recent findings suggest that under the 2006 definition of the International Astronomical Union (IAU), a dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is not a satellite. Its own gravity must pull it into a nearly round shape, and it has not cleared the neighborhood around its orbit.

According to recent reports, the IAU has so far recognized five: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris. “If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds,” Holman said.

In a recent development, icy bodies as large as 2026 ED138 are expected to be round, the Rubin release states. Whether this one is compact and round is less certain, its discoverers cautioned in their paper.

A 2019 study of a distant binary suggested that objects 250 to 620 miles (400 to 1,000 kilometers) wide mark a transition.

Smaller bodies stay porous, while larger ones have collapsed their internal voids under much higher pressures and temperatures.

According to recent reports, the discovery team estimates that about three more objects this bright, and probably more, remain undiscovered away from the Galactic plane. Rubin’s ten-year survey of the southern sky began in June 2026.

The study is available as a preprint on arXiv.

#112270. Most of the world’s lost glacier ice comes from a tiny minority of glaciers

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1121 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Most of the world’s lost glacier ice comes from a tiny minority of glaciers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A census of 216,502 glaciers finds the 3 percent that end in lakes, seas or ice shelves drive most glacier ice loss, and lakes speed it up most.
  • Outside of Earth’s two massive ice sheets, there are roughly 216,500 glaciers, and 97 percent of them end on bare rock.
  • Recent findings suggest that the other 3 percent end in a lake, the ocean, or a floating ice shelf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A census of 216,502 glaciers finds the 3 percent that end in lakes, seas or ice shelves drive most glacier ice loss, and lakes speed it up most.

Outside of Earth’s two massive ice sheets, there are roughly 216,500 glaciers, and 97 percent of them end on bare rock. Surprisingly, however, these land-based glaciers are not where most of the world’s melting ice is coming from.

Recent findings suggest that the other 3 percent end in a lake, the ocean, or a floating ice shelf. They are the ones shedding more than half of all the glacier ice lost between 2000 and 2019.

Those numbers come from a newly introduced global census of where glaciers end. Glaciers that end in lakes stood out most. Relative to their size, they lost ice about 57 percent faster than glaciers ending on land. The researchers don’t yet know why.

Joe Mallalieu did the work at the University of Birmingham and is now at the University of Leeds, with Nicholas Barrand of Birmingham among the co-authors.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mallalieu remarked the lake result was a surprise.

“What surprised us most was how much faster glaciers ending in lakes lose ice than those ending in the ocean, relative to their size,” he stated.

The team classified all 216,502 glaciers in a standard global inventory by what their fronts touch: land, a lake, the sea, or an ice shelf.

It has been revealed that earlier inventories had flagged lake-ending glaciers in only three of the world’s 19 glacier regions. The team found the rest by matching glacier outlines against a satellite map of glacial lakes built from more than 250,000 Landsat scenes.

In a recent development, then they combined that classification with existing global records of each glacier’s size, ice thickness, slope, flow speed and ice loss, plus the local climate. The full classification is public on Zenodo.

Lake-ending glaciers turned up in every one of the 19 regions. In Iceland, 65 percent of the glacier area drains to a lake, and in the southern Andes almost 40 percent does. Glaciers ending in the sea cluster in the Arctic and around Antarctica.

In a recent development, glaciers that end in lakes or the sea tend to be far bigger than those ending on land. The typical lake-ending glacier covered about eight times the area of a typical land-ending one.

It was also roughly twice as thick, about 200 feet (61 meters) against 100 feet (31 meters).

Size alone explained a lot of the ice loss but not all of it. For its size, the typical lake-ending glacier lost ice equal to a layer of water about 1.6 feet (0.49 meters) deep each year.

That is roughly double the rate at land-ending and ocean-ending glaciers.

After the team accounted for climate, elevation, slope, thickness and other factors, the gap held. Lake-ending glaciers lost about 57 percent more ice for their size than land-ending ones, and they flowed about 10 percent faster.

Ocean-ending glaciers flowed 44 percent faster than land-ending ones, yet their ice loss for their size was no higher, the authors wrote.

Recent findings suggest that lake water can remove ice from a glacier’s front in several ways. It melts the ice below the waterline, and the undercut front breaks off as icebergs.

It can also lift the front until it floats and breaks, or seep beneath the ice and reduce the friction holding it back.

Recent findings suggest that any of those would remove ice faster than melting on bare rock does. But the lake-ending glaciers in the census were also larger and flatter at their lower ends than land-ending ones.

That shape alone can slow a glacier’s adjustment to warming and keep it losing ice for longer, the authors wrote.

Mallalieu told Earth.com that even the climate difference doesn’t account for it. “And it’s not just because they tend to be in warmer, wetter places: the difference holds even when we take climate into account,” he stated.

Recent findings suggest that barrand remarked the census only became possible recently. “The last decade has seen a huge increase in the global glacier and climate data available to researchers. Bringing these datasets together lets us compare how glaciers in different settings are behaving,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that the categories themselves are moving. Glacial lakes grew by more than 50 percent in number and area between 1990 and 2018, according to a satellite survey in Nature Climate Change.

Sources indicate that many glaciers that once ended on land now end in water. Across the Arctic, meanwhile, glaciers that reached the sea are retreating onto land.

Asked by Earth.com what happens to those glaciers next, Mallalieu remarked the two switches should have opposite effects.

Glaciers pulling back onto land are likely to slow down markedly. Glaciers newly ending in lakes are likely to speed up slightly and lose ice much faster for their size.

It has been revealed that in the long run, he remarked, many lake-ending glaciers will retreat out of their lakes and end on land again. That matters for the models that project sea level rise and river flow.

According to recent reports, many of them don’t yet represent what happens where a glacier meets a lake, the authors wrote. Yet the glaciers that can respond this way hold more than half of the world’s glacier area.

The classification counts a glacier as lake-ending if any lake touches its front, however small the contact.

Glaciers with only a sliver of lake may behave more like land-ending ones, so the authors noted the real gap between the two groups is probably larger than 57 percent.

Flow speeds were available for 84 percent of glaciers and ice-loss rates for 94 percent. Furthermore, the lake map left out Svalbard and Antarctica.

Cause is also unproven: the study highlights lake-ending glaciers lose ice faster, not whether the lakes themselves are responsible.

Recent findings suggest that for communities downstream, the open question is water. Mallalieu mentioned the census did not assess water supplies. But in the Himalaya, where large populations rely on meltwater, glacier lakes are expanding fast, he said.

Better models of these glaciers would give those communities more reliable forecasts of their future water.

It has been revealed that untangling the lakes from the glacier shapes is the next task. It means measuring individual lakes, their depth, temperature and how long they persist, glacier by glacier.

Until that is done, the 57 percent is a difference the world can see and not yet explain.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#112268. Hot days with weak winds could become a major problem for the power grid

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Hot days with weak winds could become a major problem for the power grid

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Climate models project that extreme heat and weak winds will coincide more often, straining power grids as cooling demand rises and wind power drops.
  • A heat wave feels like a problem of too much: too much sun, too much demand for air conditioning.
  • For a grid that leans on wind turbines, the problem is also too little.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate models project that extreme heat and weak winds will coincide more often, straining power grids as cooling demand rises and wind power drops.

A heat wave feels like a problem of too much: too much sun, too much demand for air conditioning.

For a grid that leans on wind turbines, the problem is also too little.

When extreme heat coincides with unusually weak winds, wind farms can generate less electricity just as demand for air conditioning rises.

A upcoming analysis of 27 climate models projects that these spells of extreme heat and weak winds will become two to eight and a half times more frequent over the world’s land by 2100.

How much more depends on how much carbon dioxide is emitted.

The models also project that the longest such spell each year could last roughly two to four times as long.

Lu Shen and colleagues at Peking University in Beijing led the work, with Meng Qu as first author.

The results are model projections, not measurements, and the range reflects both the emissions path and real disagreement among the models.

Industry observers note that the team defined a bad day by two thresholds. The wind at 33 feet (10 meters) had to fall into the slowest 5% of warm-season days while the temperature rose into the hottest 5%.

It has been revealed that if heat and calm were unrelated, such days would be rare by chance alone. They aren’t unrelated.

Across the middle and high latitudes, hotter days tend to be calmer.

In parts of the northern high latitudes, Southeast Asia and northern Africa, the two coincided five to eight times more often than chance would predict in a NASA weather record.

Recent findings suggest that from 1980 to 2014, the average patch of land saw about 0.6 such days a year. Russia, the southeastern coasts of the United States and China, and parts of the tropics saw 1.5 to 3 days.

Along the storm tracks between 35 and 65 degrees north, the longest spells ran more than five days.

A spell that long means most of a week of weak wind in the middle of a heat wave, in some of the most densely populated regions on Earth.

Europe’s summer of 2022 is the authors’ example. Persistent heat and weak winds coincided with surging electricity demand and rising prices.

The projections come from a NASA dataset that sharpens 27 global climate models to a grid of about 15 miles (25 kilometers).

Each model was scored against its own 1980 to 2014 climate, so the thresholds for “hot” and “calm” shift with the model rather than with the real world.

The models project more days of extreme heat and unusually weak winds by 2100, with the largest increase under the highest-emissions pathway.

Under the lowest pathway, the rise levels off after mid-century.

The tropics change fastest. Between 30 degrees south and 30 degrees north, the frequency rises by 188% under the lowest pathway and by 934% under the highest. The northern mid-latitudes rise by 106% and 689%.

According to recent reports, the spells get longer as well as more common. By 2100, the models project that the longest such spell each year could last 84% to 315% longer worldwide, depending on the emissions pathway.

According to recent reports, the team split the increase into four causes: hotter average temperatures, slower average winds, bigger swings in both, and a tighter link between heat and calm. Warming alone accounted for most of the rise in every latitude band.

Winds change differently by region. Between 30 and 60 degrees north, average winds slow by up to 0.07 miles per hour (0.03 meters per second) a decade.

The authors tie that stilling to the Arctic warming faster than the tropics, which flattens the temperature difference that drives wind.

In the tropics, winds pick up slightly, which offsets part of the warming effect.

Industry observers note that the jet stream matters too. The models shift the northern jet about 1.6 degrees poleward by 2100. North of roughly 50 degrees, that shift strengthens the pairing of hot days with calm ones, and south of it the pairing weakens.

Twenty-seven models disagree, sometimes widely. To shrink the spread, the team checked which models best reproduced the observed trend in these compound events from 1980 to 2014.

Eight reanalysis datasets supplied the observed trend, and the projections were weighted accordingly.

The correction trimmed the projected global increase by 10% to 25% and cut the disagreement among models by 13% to 24%. The models that track history best now carry more weight, and the forecast tightens.

At the regional level it cut disagreement by 10% to 40%, raising projections for South Asia and Eastern Europe and lowering them for Southeast Asia and New Zealand.

The analysis uses daily averages, and the authors note that averaging smooths away the calmest hours, so the study likely undercounts the most extreme lulls.

The models also underestimate how tightly heat and calm are coupled in the northern high latitudes, which is where the events are most pronounced.

The stakes the authors describe are already visible. In the eastern United States, the PJM grid hit a peak load of 162.7 gigawatts during the July 2026 heat wave, close to its summer record.

Recent findings suggest that india set a demand record of 270.73 gigawatts in May 2026, with outages in places. Europe’s June 2026 heat wave was linked to more than 10,000 excess deaths.

The authors flag the hours after sunset. Solar output disappears while demand stays high, and nights are expected to warm faster than days. European minimums already exceed 68°F (20°C) on so-called tropical nights.

The authors’ answer is long-duration storage to carry daytime solar power into those evenings, more mixing of renewable sources, and above all a lower emissions path.

In their projections, the odds of a spell of extreme heat and weak winds by 2100 are four to eight times higher under the higher-emissions pathways than under the lowest one.

What the models can’t yet say is how often the calmest hours, rather than the calmest days, will coincide with the hottest ones.

Answering that would take hourly projections the downscaled dataset doesn’t provide.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#112267. Blood proteins may flag prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1294 w)

General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Blood proteins may flag prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Oxford found men's blood differed 15 years before a prostate cancer blood test or diagnosis, with an immune protein among the clearest signs.
  • According to recent reports, the blood test men know for prostate cancer measures one protein, PSA, which is made by the prostate itself.
  • The men diagnosed with prostate cancer more than 15 years later already differed in a dozen of them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oxford found men's blood differed 15 years before a prostate cancer blood test or diagnosis, with an immune protein among the clearest signs.

According to recent reports, the blood test men know for prostate cancer measures one protein, PSA, which is made by the prostate itself. In blood drawn from about 2,500 European men in the 1990s, researchers at Oxford measured more than 6,000 proteins instead.

The men diagnosed with prostate cancer more than 15 years later already differed in a dozen of them.

One of the clearest differences was an immune protein those men had less of, not more. None of the proteins is ready to become a test, the team said. Most of the differences were modest, and not all of them held up in other groups of men.

Zhe Huang, a postdoctoral epidemiologist at Oxford Population Health, part of the University of Oxford, led the work with senior authors Karl Smith-Byrne and Ruth Travis.

Industry observers note that “Prostate cancer is not one disease. Many prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause harm, while others are aggressive and can be life-threatening,” Huang remarked.

The samples came from EPIC, a European health study that recruited more than half a million people in the 1990s and stored their blood.

It has been revealed that huang’s team picked 982 men from Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and the United Kingdom who later developed prostate cancer. They compared them with a random sample of 1,573 men from the same study, followed for a median of about 16 years.

Sources indicate that men who developed the disease were a median of about six years older when they gave their blood. So the analysis adjusted for age, along with body mass index, smoking, drinking and education.

The idea was to compare the blood itself, not the men’s ages.

A lab platform called SomaScan measured more than 6,400 proteins in each sample. The team asked which proteins differed years ahead of any diagnosis, and separately which differed ahead of an aggressive cancer.

Aggressive meant high grade, spread beyond the prostate, a very high PSA at diagnosis, or death from the disease, and 290 men fit that definition.

Sources indicate that the researchers linked twelve proteins to prostate cancer diagnosed more than 15 years after the blood draw. The clearest was GZMK, a protein made by the immune cells that recognize and destroy abnormal cells.

Men with more GZMK in their blood were less likely to be diagnosed, and the longer the gap to diagnosis, the stronger that link became.

Recent findings suggest that the authors offered two readings. More GZMK may mean the immune system is doing a better job of clearing early abnormal cells.

Or the men who later developed cancer may have had fewer of those cells in the blood because the cells had moved into the prostate.

In an interview with Earth.com, Huang and Smith-Byrne stated researchers generally consider prostate cancer an immunologically “cold” tumor, one that tends to draw a weak immune response.

“This raises interesting questions about the role of the immune system in the very early stages of cancer development,” they added.

Two proteins tied to inflammation, IL-17B and OSCAR, ran the other way. Higher levels went with higher long-term risk.

Recent findings suggest that seven proteins were linked to aggressive prostate cancer. Researchers linked one of them, ANKRD1, to every serious form of the disease examined. These included cancers that had spread and cancers that proved fatal, the authors wrote.

Another, AMIGO2, linked to aggressive disease, and most strongly to cancers that had grown beyond the prostate.

This is an adhesion molecule, part of how cells attach to their surroundings, and lab studies have tied it to the process by which tumor cells break away and travel.

FLT4, a receptor involved in growing upcoming blood and lymph vessels, was linked to nearly every outcome the team measured.

Recent findings suggest that the strongest single protein was KLK3, which is PSA under its gene name. Higher PSA levels years earlier increased a man’s likelihood of receiving a diagnosis later.

That isn’t surprising, the authors wrote, because a high PSA reading is what sends a man for a biopsy in the first place.

According to recent reports, the team also looked at 71 genes already known to drive prostate cancer when they mutate, and asked whether the proteins those genes produce showed up differently in blood. Five did.

Proteins made by three of those genes, ERBB3, KRAS and NRAS, were linked to aggressive cancers diagnosed about a decade later.

The driver-gene result was the one that surprised the two researchers most.

“These genes are well established in prostate cancer biology, so it was quite surprising to find that their circulating protein products were associated with aggressive prostate cancer,” Huang and Smith-Byrne said.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t mean the cancer was already there when the blood was drawn, the authors wrote. Nor is a protein level in blood proof that the gene itself has gone wrong.

Their reading is that the proteins mark early disturbances in the biological pathways to which those genes belong.

The team checked its findings against a U.S. study of 4,284 men, 590 of whom developed prostate cancer. Only about half of the proteins had been measured there.

Two of them, KLK3 and ACP3, another prostate protein, were clearly linked to the disease there too, and two more revealed the same direction of association.

Several others, including OSCAR, AMIGO2 and FLT4, were associated in opposite directions in Black and White men. The U.S. study had too few Black participants to settle which direction is real, the authors wrote.

In the U.K. Biobank, 18 of the proteins had been measured with a different technology, and the two platforms agreed poorly.

None of those proteins was linked to prostate cancer there. Genetic analyses supported a handful, including AMIGO2, KLK3 and OSCAR.

The aggressive-cancer results also come from fewer men. Tumor grade was unknown for 31 percent of the cases and stage for 46 percent, and only 102 men died of the disease.

Some of the associations may be chance, the authors wrote, and the study had no information on family history.

Whether any of these blood proteins can predict a man’s prostate cancer risk better than his age and PSA already do hasn’t been tested.

The findings still have to be confirmed in larger and more diverse groups of men, Huang and Smith-Byrne stated. Their study also mainly looked for proteins that may help a prostate cancer develop, not proteins that could spot a cancer already there.

“Developing a blood test for early detection would require further dedicated prediction studies,” they told Earth.com.

Huang said measuring thousands of proteins in blood collected years early lets researchers begin to ask how men who later develop aggressive prostate cancer differ from men who don’t.

The next step runs through a Cancer Research U.K. program on prostate cancer causes and prevention, which the team mentioned will test whether the findings can improve prediction or prevention.

Some of the proteins may even play a causal role in how the cancer develops, the two researchers remarked.

“If confirmed by future experimental and clinical studies, this could open up exciting opportunities for earlier prevention, potentially even through approaches such as cancer vaccines,” they said.

For now, the GZMK result is a clue rather than a tool. Men who were never diagnosed had more of an immune protein in their blood 15 years earlier. Whether measuring it would help any patient is the question still open.

The full study was published in the journal European Urology.

Scientists can now uncover a person’s age, sex, diet, and DNA all from just one single tooth

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1387 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Forensic scientists sliced a single tooth from each of 15 unidentified bodies and read birth year, age, sex, DNA, diet, and drug use from it.
  • By the time a body is discovered months or years after death, the face, fingerprints, and clothing are usually long gone.
  • Industry observers note that A team in Japan took a single tooth from each of 15 such bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Forensic scientists sliced a single tooth from each of 15 unidentified bodies and read birth year, age, sex, DNA, diet, and drug use from it.

By the time a body is discovered months or years after death, the face, fingerprints, and clothing are usually long gone. The remaining bones can give investigators a rough idea of sex and age, but that age estimate can be wrong by up to 30 years. Turns out, a single tooth holds far more answers.

Industry observers note that A team in Japan took a single tooth from each of 15 such bodies. From that tooth alone, they worked out each person’s birth year, age at death, sex, and DNA profile.

The same tooth also showed what kind of diet the person grew up on and which drugs they had been taking.

Hisako Saitoh, an associate professor of forensic dentistry at the Institute of Science Tokyo, led the work with her doctoral student, Sayaka Yamada.

It has been revealed that fuyuki Tokanai of the Center for Accelerator Mass Spectrometry at Yamagata University was also on the team. Colleagues at the University of Tokyo and Chiba University took part as well.

Sources indicate that all 15 people were unidentified when they reached the autopsy table. Five were skeletal remains, ten were badly decomposed. Fourteen of them were later identified.

Industry observers note that “Different tissues within a tooth preserve different forensic information. By combining multiple analytical methods, we sought to obtain as many clues as possible from a single tooth,” Saitoh remarked.

Bone is full of tiny channels for blood vessels and marrow. This means that soil, moisture, and microbes can get into it after death. Enamel is the hardest material in the human body, and it seals the crown of a tooth.

A thin layer called cementum wraps around the root, and this keeps outside substances away from the soft pulp inside.

A tooth also stops changing once it has formed. Bone rebuilds itself throughout life, but enamel laid down in early childhood stays chemically the same until death.

Industry observers note that that makes a tooth a sealed record of the years when it grew. This explains why researchers have used teeth to track where a mammoth or an elephant once lived.

Earlier forensic teams had combined several of these tests, but they used several teeth per person, or a tooth plus a toenail, and the bodies hadn’t been dead for long.

Saitoh’s team wanted to know how much information one tooth could provide after a body had been lying outdoors for months or years.

Industry observers note that the team chose the lower first premolar, the tooth just behind the canine. Its crown finishes forming at about age five, so its enamel records the first years of life. It has a single root, it’s easy to pull, and the lips cover the gap it leaves.

Each tooth was washed, dried overnight, and cut lengthwise into slices about 1/25 of an inch (1 millimeter) thick, which is thinner than a dime.

According to recent reports, enamel from one slice went to a radiocarbon lab, and a root slice rich in cementum went to DNA testing. Dentin from the other side went to an age test, and the central slice holding the pulp went to drug screening.

In a recent development, the age test relies on a slow chemical change. Amino acids in living tissue come in a left-handed form, and over a lifetime a small share flips to the right-handed mirror image.

The team measured that share in the dentin and read the person’s age off a curve built from six other premolars of known age.

The birth year came from radiocarbon, but not the kind used on fossils. Nuclear weapons tests in the 1950s and early 1960s sharply raised the amount of radioactive carbon in the air. The level peaked in 1963 and has been falling ever since.

In a recent development, enamel forming in a child’s mouth took up whatever level was in the air at the time, so its carbon indicates when it formed. Scientists have used the same spike to age a whale from its teeth.

Industry observers note that the catch is that the curve rises and then falls, so one reading usually matches two possible years. For one man, the enamel gave a birth year of either 1955 or 1979.

Recent findings suggest that adding the age-at-death estimate settled it. A birth in 1979 plus his estimated 58 years would put his death in 2036, so he was born in 1955. His real birth year was 1957.

Across the 15 people, the radiocarbon ranges included the true birth year in 14 cases. The age-at-death estimates on their own were off by about eight years on average.

Once the two tests were combined, the birth-year estimates landed within about five years of the truth, on average.

Sources indicate that DNA from the cementum slice gave the person’s sex in all 15 cases. In 12 of them it also produced a profile with enough genetic markers to match against a relative or a database.

The same kind of DNA work has recently corrected the story of a Roman-era skeleton in England and been read from Neanderthal teeth.

In a recent development, the pulp slice went through a drug screen covering 251 substances, and every one of the 15 teeth contained something, even if only caffeine. In nine cases the drugs in the tooth matched at least some of what the original autopsy had found in blood or muscle.

In five cases they matched prescriptions the person was known to have been taking, including antidepressants and antipsychotics.

The tooth didn’t catch everything, however. Drugs that appeared to have been taken shortly before death highlighted up in stomach contents and muscle at autopsy but not in the tooth.

Saitoh’s team suggested that drugs move into a tooth slowly, so a tooth reflects long-term use rather than a last dose.

The fifteenth body belonged to a man who has never been definitively identified. His tooth put his birth year at either 1956 or 1976, and his dentin put his age at about 38.

The 1956 option would mean he died in 1995, long before his body was found in 2013, so the team’s answer is a man born in 1976.

It has been revealed that investigators right now believe he was born around 1972 and was about 41 when he died. The two readings disagree by four years, which is inside the method’s average error of about five years.

The tooth gives investigators a second, independent estimate of who he might be.

Industry observers note that stable carbon in the enamel added a rough picture of childhood diet. All 15 readings fit a diet built on rice and wheat rather than corn, which is consistent with a traditional Japanese diet.

The authors wrote that carbon alone can’t say where someone grew up.

It has been revealed that the errors here were larger than in earlier studies that ran each test on its own. The birth-year estimates were least accurate for people born before the fallout spike began to climb and for those born in more recent years, when the curve had flattened.

It has been revealed that the age test usually works best on dentin from the center of the tooth. Here the center was needed for the drug screen. Instead, the team used dentin from the outer part, and that may have cost some accuracy.

One tooth also produced radiocarbon dates between the 600s and 800s AD, centuries before the woman could have been born.

That sample had the highest carbon content of the set, and the authors suspect carbon from outside the body had got into the enamel.

The team’s next step is more cases, and a closer look at exactly where in a tooth each slice should come from.

“Moving forward, we aim to further improve the accuracy and reproducibility of each biochemical analytical method demonstrated in this study and establish standardized methods that can be widely applied in routine forensic medical and dental practice,” Saitoh mentioned.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

According to recent reports, the finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she claims, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

Sources indicate that “This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi indicates. “It’s growing so promptly, the field itself.”.

#112263. Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1406 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Ice Age humans were far less isolated than scientists assumed, according to a 30,000-year-old woman’s DNA

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1406 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.
  • Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.
  • Archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ice Age Europeans mixed across the continent earlier than genetics had shown, according to a 30,000-year-old genome and DNA from cave dirt.

Most people imagine Ice Age Europe as a patchwork of tiny hunting bands living out their lives in isolated valleys, far from any other group.

Archaeologists have doubted that version of history for a long time. This is mainly due to the fact that the same styles of tools and carvings show up across the entire continent. Even so, DNA from Ice Age samples has mostly supported the isolated view.

A woman who died around 30,000 years ago in what is now southwestern France has changed that.

In a recent development, most of her ancestry came from the western European people of her time. However, part of it also came from populations related to central and eastern Europe. The mixing happened roughly 32,500 to 31,500 years ago.

The analysis of her DNA now gives the oldest set of genome-wide data from a modern human in southwestern Europe.

Pere Gelabert and Ron Pinhasi of the University of Vienna‘s Department of Evolutionary Anthropology led the work. Their co-authors include researchers at Harvard Medical School, the University of Cantabria and the University of Upcoming Mexico.

The study rests on DNA from three new Ice Age individuals and one sample of cave sediment. Thus, the picture it draws is built from very few people.

In a recent development, the bone fragment of the woman was recovered from Isturitz Cave in the Basque Country, western Pyrenees. Excavators dug it up in the 1950s, and it stayed in a Paris institute for over 60 years. Then, in 2013, Pinhasi took a sample from it for DNA analysis.

The team recovered more than 454,000 of the genetic markers it was looking for. This represents one of the richest Gravettian datasets yet.

Gravettian is the name for the culture that spread across Europe during the onset of the last Ice Age, between about 34,000 and 25,000 years ago. This culture is known for its shared tool styles, burial practices and portable art.

Until now, DNA data from this Ice Age period in Europe sorted into two stable groups, a western one and a central-eastern one, with little sign of contact between them.

It has been revealed that the Isturitz woman belongs mostly to the western group. But several tests also found a share of her ancestry related to the ancestors of people buried at Dolní Věstonice in what is now the Czech Republic.

In an interview with Earth.com, Gelabert said the find overturned a long-held assumption.

“Until this new genomic data, we assumed that the people in Southwestern Europe were quite the same for more than 20,000 years,” he stated.

The new data, he stated, point to population movements that were probably continental in scale, and that the team doesn’t yet clearly understand.

Isturitz is one of the richest Ice Age sites in southern Europe, with an unusual number of carved objects and signs of repeated, intensive occupation.

It has been revealed that archaeologists have long argued that it was a gathering place where different groups met to hunt, trade, socialize and find partners. The cave lies at the natural passage between the rest of Europe and the Iberian Peninsula.

Industry observers note that the woman isn’t alone. When the team reanalyzed a previously published genome from Ormesson, near Paris, dated to about 31,800 to 30,000 years ago, it found a similar eastern signal.

In addition, Belgian individuals from Goyet Cave, about 28,000 to 26,000 years old, were already known to carry mixed ancestry.

Recent findings suggest that two explanations are possible, the authors wrote. People from the east may have moved west during the Gravettian itself. Or the eastern-looking ancestry may be an older component, already in western Europe before 35,000 years ago.

Industry observers note that the team favors the first. The DNA signal is absent from earlier Ice Age genomes in the same region, and it vanishes from southwestern Europe after 30,000 years ago.

At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, northern Spain, the team took two pinches of sediment, 0.002 ounces (50 milligrams) each.

Industry observers note that they came from a layer dated to about 22,100 to 21,700 years ago, the coldest stretch of the last Ice Age, when human remains are extremely rare. No bone or tooth was needed, only the dirt that people had walked on.

The researchers built nine DNA libraries from those two extracts and sequenced them 101 times. Out of roughly a billion DNA fragments, more than 294,000 were human.

After the team kept only fragments showing the chemical damage of real ancient DNA, 14,737 genetic markers remained, enough to read the ancestry of the people who used the cave.

The sediment’s ancestry matched the western group, the Isturitz woman’s lineage, so that ancestry persisted in the region through the coldest millennia.

“Sedimentary DNA allows us to recover genetic information from periods where human remains are missing,” Pinhasi said. “This gives us a way to connect archaeological layers with the genetic ancestry of the people who occupied a site.”.

Gelabert told Earth.com the team had recovered DNA from this cave’s sediment before. “What surprised us this time is that the quality is unmatched,” he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that he described the sample as one of the richest sources of human DNA ever reported. For the first time in the region’s Upper Paleolithic, he noted, it let the team tie a culture to a group of people.

The third upcoming genome came from Ostuni Cave in southern Italy and belongs to a male fetus about 27,800 to 27,400 years old.

The team identified him as a first-degree relative of a woman from the same cave whose genome was already published. He was most likely her son.

Industry observers note that comparing the two revealed that his father came from the same population as his mother, as far as the data can tell. Yet the parents were not close relatives.

The boy’s genome carried no long stretches of identical DNA from both parents, and the population he came from was genetically larger than any other Gravettian group measured so far.

Gelabert noted this is the first mother-and-fetus pair of genomes from the European Paleolithic, and that comparing them is what indicated how genetically diverse her population was.

All three individuals, and the people in the El Mirón sediment, are predicted to have had dark skin, dark hair and brown eyes. That was the usual pattern for Europeans of that era.

The whole Gravettian, Solutrean and Epigravettian record, three Ice Age cultures, rests on genome-wide data from fewer than 50 people. This study adds an extra three.

In a recent development, the third is a tooth from Chufín Cave in Cantabria, dated to about 26,000 years ago. It was so degraded that it yielded fewer than 20,000 markers, enough to place it in the western group and little more.

Sources indicate that sediment has its own limits. The DNA in it comes from several people mixed together, and the team’s reading suggests more of them were male than female. The date for the east-west mixing also assumes it happened in a single pulse.

Industry observers note that the study does not settle where the eastern ancestry came from. The authors wrote that no particular central European group stands out as the source, and that no genome from the earlier Aurignacian culture exists for southwestern Europe to compare against.

Sources indicate that the team did find one thing the data argue against. Earlier work on tooth shapes had suggested a population turnover in western Europe around 28,000 years ago.

The newly introduced genomes, the sediment and the reanalyzed published data instead show the same western ancestry in place from 30,000 to 20,000 years ago.

Asked by Earth.com what comes next, Gelabert returned to the sediment.

According to recent reports, “Next step is clearly to find out when the population movements that we see in Isturitz really happened. Sediment will be key for this goal,” he stated.

The authors named a target: the Aurignacian layers of Isturitz itself, deposits older than the woman, which could show whether the eastern signal was already there before she was born.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#112262. Latest Update: Air pollution may weaken one of the brain’s natural defenses against dementia
