Review: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres (Hyatt Inclusive)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2025 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that of note, I was in Cancun, Mexico for business meetings at another resort but wanted to evaluate both this experience for our readers as well as the overall position of Hyatt in its ever-growing Inclusives collection.
  • Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an adults-only resort in the Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and I toured it on a site visit in November 2026.
  • Address: Carretera Punta Sam – Isla Blanca, Mz 2, Lt 10, Costa Mujeres, Zona Continental Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo 77400, Mexico.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that of note, I was in Cancun, Mexico for business meetings at another resort but wanted to evaluate both this experience for our readers as well as the overall position of Hyatt in its ever-growing Inclusives collection. My stay was almost exactly 24 hours and solo which is uncharacteristic at this destination resort. My experience will likely differ from other guests due to those factors.

Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an adults-only resort in the Hyatt Inclusive Collection, and I toured it on a site visit in November 2026. It sits on a stretch of white-sand beach in Costa Mujeres, 12 miles north of Cancun. Cancun International Airport is the arrival airport. I could not confirm a single official transfer time from the property page. Tour listings commonly put the drive in a 30 to 45 minute range.

Address: Carretera Punta Sam – Isla Blanca, Mz 2, Lt 10, Costa Mujeres, Zona Continental Isla Mujeres, Quintana Roo 77400, Mexico.

Google Maps: Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres.

Hyatt is the best in the business at high end resort arrivals. I had given my name at the security gate and by the time I reached the lobby, the door to the vehicle was opened for me, I was greeted by name and a “welcome home”, a constant refrain throughout my stay. It’s a small thing and maybe cliché but it was effective. I was given a Globalist upgrade even though rules at all-inclusives differ from the rest of the chain. As my upgrade was in a Preferred room, I was brought into a private room at the front of the lobby where check-in was done for me.

The lobby is an open-air room under an arched woven ceiling, with a direct view out to the ocean.

According to recent reports, the resort is spread across 10 buildings with 505 keys. Of those, 221 are Preferred Club keys with an elevated experience. My building (and others like it) had just five rooms on each floor and just five floors which made it feel boutique rather than massive. Every oceanfront room is Preferred Club, and so are the first two buildings on either side.

The room views follow a simple rule by floor. Every first floor room is a swim-out, floors two through four are tropical view, and the fifth floor is ocean view or ocean front. That makes booking easy to reason through: if you want to step off your patio into the water, go low, and if you want the sea, go high.

The walkways give a sense of grandeur and space. All of the flora is local, and in a touch I loved, the service rooms are named after the plants.

According to recent reports, there are four pools, and each one has a unique characteristic. The Jungle pool is drinks only and hidden in the middle of the resort by trees. The Social pool runs activities throughout the day at this adults-only resort for those who want to participate. There is also an infinity pool on the edge of the beach, and then the Preferred Club pool for those staying in that category. These are separate from the first floor swim-outs.

The spa (hydrotherapy is included for Preferred guests) featured an outdoor circuit that included both hot and cold plunge pools, amongst other therapeutic services.

The Preferred Club pool was the most frequented, though some images below look more vacant due to rain that rolled through during my opportunity to collect media on my short stay.

The gym is open to every guest from 6 AM to 8 PM, and it is outfitted with Technogym equipment.

The spa is open 8 AM to 8 PM with 17 treatment cabins and a beauty salon, and hydrotherapy is included. That last part is the headline. The hydrotherapy space is ridiculous, easily the standout of the entire property for me, and it is the kind of amenity that would make me pick this resort over a competitor down the beach. There are indoor and outdoor showers as well.

The men’s changing room featured private showers with an option for indoor or outdoor experiences.

The theater seats 264 people and hosts cabaret and Mayan highlights. There are also pickleball courts, which I am starting to think should be required equipment at any resort that wants a younger crowd as well as padel for the European set (and growing American interest.).

Secrets is an adults-only brand, and every room here comes with what the firm calls Unlimited-Luxury. For a standard guest that means unlimited dining and top-shelf drinks, Wi-Fi, daytime activities and nightly entertainment, with tips and taxes included. Add 24-hour room service, a mini-bar refreshed daily (you can ask for just about anything you want in there), and pool and beach wait service for all guests.

Industry observers note that the Preferred Club is an upgrade, and at this resort it is a big one because it owns the oceanfront. Secrets lists personalized check-in and check-out, afternoon hot and cold hors d’oeuvres, desserts and premium liquors, access to the Preferred Club lounge and beach bar, an upgraded mini-bar, upgraded bath amenities, butler service, Bali beds at the pool and beach reserved for club guests, and exclusive dining at the Preferred Club beach restaurant. Preferred also gives club guests exclusive access to an infinity pool and puts an oversized soaking tub on the terrace of the upgraded suites (at least with the oceanfronts).

Recent findings suggest that I book a lot of Hyatt’s all-inclusives through Hyatt Privé rates, and this resort is one of 388 in the collection. Privé is Hyatt’s invitation-only program for travel advisors, so you only get the benefits when an approved advisor makes the booking, and the stay still earns World of Hyatt points and elite nights.

In a recent development, the all-inclusive version of Privé looks a lot different from a Park Hyatt booking. As I wrote when Hyatt’s all-inclusive resorts joined Privé, there is no room upgrade and no breakfast benefit, since every meal is already included. At this property, Privé guests receive a $100 resort credit per stay, a welcome amenity and letter, hydrotherapy access, and early check-in and late check-out based on availability.

Elite status matters here more than at most all-inclusives. Under World of Hyatt’s terms, Globalists get the best room available at check-in, including rooms with club access, at the resort’s discretion. Explorists are eligible for upgrades too, but not to standard suites or club rooms. Travelers who have stayed at Secrets resorts as Globalists report being designated Preferred Club guests even when they did not land in a club building, which unlocks the lounge, pool and beach areas. This was my experience on all accounts at the resort. Late checkout is 2 PM for Explorists and 4 PM for Globalists, subject to availability at resorts. It was able to honor my request for a late check-out, I did not arrive early enough to request the early check-in. Hyatt waives resort fees on eligible paid rates (at least for now) and award nights for Globalists, and on award nights only for every other tier, and Globalists also get free parking on free nights though in 2028 Globalists will have to select this as a preference. One catch is that Suite Upgrade Awards cannot be used at Secrets resorts, so you cannot lock in a suite with one here.

Recent findings suggest that weddings are big business here. The courtyard outside the theater is the setting, with the sunset behind it, and the resort hosts lots of them. The resort disclosed its occupancy to me but it wasn’t clear if it was for public consumption. It was shockingly high especially for a Thursday in mid-November. Over the holidays or spring break all the hotels are full but this is a period where I would have expected a lull. Still, despite being extremely full, it never felt crowded.

In a recent development, for meetings and groups, the convention space measures 9,800 square feet and splits into five sections. The boardroom was occupied at the time so I couldn’t include images of that.

According to recent reports, restaurants can be booked in advance through the Hyatt Inclusive Collection app, which I wish more all-inclusives offered. Nobody wants to find out at 7 PM that the restaurant they wanted is full and through the app this can be done well in advance of a guest’s arrival. The dress code in the restaurants is resort casual, though the patio does not require slacks and closed toed shoes for men, shorts are acceptable outside.

Sources indicate that the restaurants include: Portofino (Italian), Bordeaux (French), Himitsu (pan-Asian, with sushi and teppanyaki), Oceana (seafood in an open-air setting), Barefoot Grill (light lunch), Market Café (the international buffet, which I noted on site as the Marketplace), Seaside Grill (a poolside grill), and Coco Café. The bars on that list include Rendezvous in the lobby, Barracuda on the beach, a swim-up bar, a beach bar, and the Preferred Club beach bar and lounge bar. There’s also a Sports Bar and Lounge next to the theater.

Oceana is the seafood restaurant, set in an open-air dining room with woven pendant lamps, macrame hangings and a pebble mosaic floor. I chose this for my one dinner on property during my brief stay.

Recent findings suggest that I started with the lamb croquettes, which the menu serves with yogurt and sweet chili sauce, cashews, watercress and a pickled shallot salad, and the Iberian salad with fresh mozzarella, prosciutto, rucula, toasted pistachios, balsamic and roasted peach. A crusty loaf came with the meal.

For a main I had the coconut shrimp, served with parsley orzo pasta, coconut sauce and parmesan crispy, and finished with the mango cheesecake, which the menu plates with vanilla cream and a mango compote with honey and basil.

Market Café, the international buffet I noted as the Marketplace, serves breakfast until 11:30 AM. [TO CONFIRM: lunch and dinner service at Market Café].

Recent findings suggest that seaside Grill hosts the Preferred Club à la carte breakfast. The official dining page notes breakfast there is served for Preferred Club guests only. I tried a number of dishes for lunch to report to our fine audience.

Rendezvous sits at the heart of the property with 360-degree access, so you can walk up to it from any direction.

Preferred Club guests get their own bar at the beach, and the Preferred Club lounge also has an indoor lounge for when the sun gets to be too much.

Sources indicate that my room was a Preferred Oceanfront King, a single open room with a king bed against a macrame headboard wall, rattan pendant lights, a ceiling fan, and a daybed sofa facing a marble bistro table. The balcony with jacuzzi looks straight over the beach. In the bathroom, a freestanding tub sits under a wood-slat ceiling beside a walk-in rain shower with a pebble floor and a bench. The double vanity has vessel sinks, round mirrors and a wave-textured wall, and the shower is stocked with Le Labo Bergamote 22 shampoo, conditioner and shower gel. Le Labo is a confirmed winner for me.

I also had the chance to tour a master suites, all of which are oceanfront, and they are also available as swim-outs.

Every first floor room is a swim-out, opening onto the pool.

It has been revealed that secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres is an incredible resort that somehow felt small when you were in your building but big enough to have everything. For my stay, I used 45,000 points on a no-notice booking to offset a $1,300/night stay. I have seen rates from $560 for off-season which is without question worth it. I loved the property and I look forward to returning with more time and my wife, but the adults-only nature of the property will make it a harder stay for us to achieve.

What do you think? Have you stayed at Secrets Playa Blanca Costa Mujeres?

Latest Update: Editorial: JetBlue Status Match Made Clear It’s Not For Me

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, last June, JetBlue launched a status match that put elites from competing carriers into Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2.
  • My application was approved just before the June 30 deadline.
  • My two primary airports are Pittsburgh, PA (PIT) and Fort Myers, FL (RSW).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last June, JetBlue launched a status match that put elites from competing carriers into Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2. It also offered a faster track for Delta Diamond, Delta 360, AA Executive Platinum and Concierge Key members: earn 50 tiles by year-end and get Mosaic 4. That worked out to $5,000 in JetBlue flights or Paisly packages, or $50,000 on the JetBlue card, and a single Mint roundtrip to Europe could cover most of it. I already had AA Executive Platinum, so I didn’t need the status. I wanted it anyway. JetBlue was adding routes from my home airports, I fly to Boston, Latest York and Fort Lauderdale often, and the United partnership raised the possibility of benefits on both sides.

My application was approved just before the June 30 deadline. Some applicants waited up to six weeks for processing, though, and losing six weeks of a 12-week challenge is a real cost. JetBlue then added its 25-for-25 promotion on top. Visiting 25 destinations by year-end earned up to 350,000 TrueBlue points plus 25 years of Mosaic 1, which made a cheap, aggressive weekend of short hops look worth it. My initiative was to finish the challenge through spend and put the points toward transatlantic and Japan trips. My one worry at the time was whether JetBlue would treat these latest Mosaics well enough to keep them flying with it.

My two primary airports are Pittsburgh, PA (PIT) and Fort Myers, FL (RSW). I occasionally also fly from Fort Lauderdale or Miami when it makes sense. But Pittsburgh had just flights to Boston for some of last year, before adding Fort Lauderdale to fill the Spirit gap and then Upcoming York JFK competing with Delta, and more broadly to the New York market, United and American with more than enough flights. From Fort Myers, it’s Boston of JFK.

I flew once to Boston on JetBlue but at the time, it had not yet launched a domestic first class, a better seat selection included in my fare was the only real enhancement to the short flight of just over 80 minutes. I’ll cover other reasons why I wasn’t able to fly the carrier more, but given that I am not in Newly introduced York, Boston, or Fort Lauderdale full time, every flight I take has a connection and it’s not particularly on-the-way for me. For example, if heading south to Florida, Charlotte, Atlanta, or even Washington Dulles make more sense than Boston or New York but when heading west at all, Chicago, Houston, Dallas, and Denver are all obviously better options.

Even to Europe, there’s not a material advantage with limited schedules and limited footprint on the continent. For trips to Paris given that I will have to connect anyway, I have more options on any other carrier through east coast hubs than with JetBlue on its metal not to mention partner networks.

Industry observers note that most recently, I had a flight to Cancun and with airport time, flight time and connections, it’s faster to fly out of Miami or Fort Lauderdale. But JetBlue had fewer flights for more money and far more miles than with American. Outside of the northeast corridor or based in South(east) Florida, I couldn’t make it make sense.

Recent findings suggest that I’m heading to Europe for a meeting next week and I will finally have a chance to try Mint. This will constitute two of my longest flights with JetBlue ever. I haven’t heard many negative comments about JetBlue Mint, and I have high expectations. It’s hard to get excited about another American or United flight in business class solely because I have flown those so often and there’s little new there.

Industry observers note that I’ll get a chance to try a reasonably long three-hour flight domestically to see how it differs from my prior JetBlue experience. Then, assuming flights are on time, I should have a chance to try the newly introduced BlueHouse, a first for me. Following that is a long haul flight in Mint and I am looking forward to the experience.

Statistically, I can’t see a reason that I try for Mosaic again, but who knows? The experience could change what appears to be a clear analytical decision for me at this point.

One of the biggest reasons I secure status via flying/spending/staying is to redeem systemwide upgrades (or suite upgrades in the case of hotels.) I’ll fully admit that upon receiving approval for the challenge last year, I hadn’t even considered that Mint certificates would work differently than other upgrade certificates in the industry. One upgrade certificate is worth an upgrade (if available.) United uses “Plus Points” but it feels clearer that there will be some variability in what’s required to move between the cabins.

For this particular trip, JetBlue wanted two upgrade certificates in one direction, and four on another. Thankfully, I had taken the upgrade option every time I achieved a choice to select a benefit, but had I chosen something else assuming that I’d only need two Move to Mint certificates (as I would with American for example) I would have come up short.

Industry observers note that I covered how much spending is required to achieve top tier status and its associated benefits in recent posts. This was in response to United’s move to require $480,000 in annual spending (by credit card only) to achieve United 1K status. Assuming that along the way loyalty points are taken and annual Mosaic bonuses are applied to cardholders, JetBlue is above American at $225,000 in spend for Mosaic 4 vs. American’s net of $164,000 for Executive Platinum with just two systemwide upgrades, or $214,000 with six. The difference is that those six upgrades apply for the full-one-way on a single certificate.

I spent time trying to figure out why one way charged four Move to Mint vs two and in the end, it didn’t really matter. I can nearly upgrade my entire family of four on American vs a single roundtrip for myself. For what it’s worth, the base cost was also more expensive with JetBlue than American for which I had upgrades available.

I have the qualified business spend to earn Mosaic 4 every year, but the value of its perks aren’t even close to the rest of the market. And for what JetBlue expects in spend compared to what I could earn elsewhere is uncompetitive.

And as a side note, the fixed rate of JetBlue points (about 1.4¢/each) is unimpressive but for most of the attempts I tried to use them throughout the year both domestically and internationally, they proved of little value. A lack of partners is much the same. I looked at a redemption in Mint on my flights to Europe and though I had more than 220,000, it was an insufficient balance for the simple roundtrip. For context, I took United a few years ago on miles and redeemed 160,000 roundtrip (this year was available at 176,000 roundtrip) and multiple times in the last 24 months on American at or around 115,000 roundtrip. Miles aren’t worth enough, they aren’t flexible enough, and there aren’t enough partners to fill gaps in the JetBlue map.

I had higher expectations for JetBlue based on the experiences of my peers. I think its equipment is excellent, but widespread first class availability is a necessity. The limited utility of Move to Mint certificates were the nail in the coffin and the usability of the miles didn’t help. But even then, I really want to love and fly JetBlue, and I am willing to go a little out of my way to use them. But I’m not willing to fly backwards for fewer flights at a higher cost.

Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor.
  • Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.
  • The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.).

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

In a recent development, comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”.

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

According to recent reports, the county unveiled this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

The airline prepares to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

“Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano noted in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.
